quote: Newly minted quadriplegics are not as sad, six months later, as they expect to be, etc.
content: The essay's words are "not as sad, six months later, as they expect to be." That is Brickman's result as Fable states it: the gap was real but smaller than outsiders predicted. Lucas is right that adaptation to lasting disability is partial, and "Quadriplegics deal" should be read as coping, not as recovery. The general mechanism is well supported. People overpredict how long their distress will last because they neglect the psychological immune system that goes to work after a blow (Gilbert et al. 1998). As Fable says, the technique needs only that the feared state be survivable and less bad than it looks from outside. Both halves of that are what the data show.

quote: Be a true coward, and plan out your retreat in detail—visualize every step—preferably before you first come to the battlefield.
content: Fable endorses the technique and cites its support: Oettingen's mental contrasting, defensive pessimism, and decatastrophizing. On the final question, the premise the technique targets is documented. Across thirteen countries, people intuitively take serial killers to be atheists far more readily than believers, even in secular countries and even among atheist respondents (Gervais et al. 2017). A believer who pictures atheism pictures that villain. A line of retreat replaces it with an accurate picture, "I would go on being moral anyway," and the essay marks its closing sentence as a question, not a forecast.
